title: Linear-space LZ77 random access
formal: Do there exist uniform deterministic preprocessing and query algorithms and absolute constants \(C,K>0\), integers \(a\ge1,b\ge2\), such that, for every string \(S\in[1..N]^N\) with \(N\ge1\), its greedy overlapping LZ77 parse with \(z\) phrases can be preprocessed in at most \(K(N+1)^a\) bit operations into a representation supporting every character query \(i\in[1..N]\) with exact answer \(S[i]\), worst-case query time at most \(C(1+\log_2 N)\), and at most \(Cz\) machine words in total at query time? A word has \(w=b\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) bits, and query time counts the word-RAM operations below.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of a uniform scheme with all the stated construction, space, correctness and worst-case query bounds, or a complete Lean proof that no such scheme exists in this model. Space proportional to a larger grammar or to an LZ-End or LZBE parse is insufficient unless the required bound in terms of this greedy LZ77 phrase count is also established. The target is exact access with asymptotic resource guarantees, not numerical approximation of a character.
why: Random access is a basic interface for computation on compressed texts. Linear storage in the LZ77 phrase count would preserve the benefit of repetition while making individual characters accessible without expanding the text.
definitions:
The notation \([1..N]\) means the integers from 1 to \(N\). The input is \(N\) and a list of phrases, each either a literal character or a pair consisting of a source position and a positive length. Each tag, character, position and length occupies a constant number of words and is given explicitly in binary. The phrases concatenate to \(S\). At an unparsed position \(p\), if \(S[p]\) has no earlier occurrence, the next phrase is that literal. Otherwise its length is the maximum \(\ell\le N-p+1\) such that there exists \(s<p\) with
\[
S[s..s+\ell-1]=S[p..p+\ell-1].
\]
The copied phrase stores any such source \(s\); every choice among tied sources is allowed. Copying is sequential: its \(j\)-th character is the character already decoded at position \(s+j\), for \(0\le j<\ell\). Thus a source may overlap the destination. The input promise is a valid greedy parse in this convention; malformed encodings need no guarantee. The phrase count \(z\), rather than the uncompressed length or a different parser's output size, is the space parameter.

Preprocessing is performed by one deterministic multitape Turing machine on the binary input. Its polynomial bound is in the uncompressed length \(N\); it need not be polynomial in the shorter compressed input length. Temporary preprocessing storage and even decompression are allowed within that time, but only the final representation is retained for queries. This preserves the existing card's polynomial-in-\(N\) construction convention; the source's brief question does not separately prescribe a compressed-time construction bound.

The query algorithm is one fixed finite word-RAM program. Registers and memory cells hold \(w\)-bit unsigned integers. Unit-cost operations are copying, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, left and right shifts, unsigned comparisons, conditional branches, and reading or writing a word at an address stored in a word. Left shifts discard high bits, right shifts fill with zeros, and shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. An operation uses only a fixed constant number of words; longer computations pay for every operation. Access to a precomputed table is allowed only when its storage is charged.

Each query begins with the retained representation and its index and must return the exact character. The space bound includes all retained input, auxiliary tables, query work cells and registers. Any information about \(N\), phrase boundaries or the alphabet must fit there. All query computations count, and the bound applies to every query, not merely to an average over positions. The uncompressed string is unavailable except to the extent encoded in the charged representation. The algorithms have no advice, randomness, oracle or uncharged global table. The constants and programs are independent of \(N,z,S\) and the query position; the fixed word-size multiplier \(b\) is part of the scheme.

progress.text: Grammar balancing with constant-factor size growth is established at FOCS 2019 and in the JACM 2021 publication.
The Dagstuhl question asks for linear-space logarithmic-time access to Lempel–Ziv compressed strings.
The CPM paper obtains logarithmic access in linear space for the restricted LZBE representation.
The ICALP grammar trade-off paper explicitly distinguishes the remaining ordinary-LZ77 linear-space question.
The LZ-End preprint gives deterministic construction and improved access bounds for that different parsing scheme.
Completed the uniform word-RAM and preprocessing formulation and checked later results without transferring bounds between different compression parameters.

context_blocks.text: Section 5.4 asks for storage linear in the Lempel–Ziv representation and logarithmic-time character indexing. This card retains the existing deterministic, greedy, overlapping-LZ77 interpretation, integer alphabet and polynomial-in-uncompressed-length preprocessing, and spells out the previously implicit word operations and quantifiers.

A straight-line grammar is a finite acyclic set of concatenation rules generating exactly one string. Ganardi, Jeż and Lohrey prove that a supplied grammar can be balanced with only constant-factor growth, giving logarithmic access in space proportional to its grammar size. That parameter can be larger than the greedy LZ77 phrase count.

The July 2026 LZ-End paper reports the familiar classical-LZ77 bound \(O(z(1+\log(N/z)))\) in space and retains linear-space efficient access as a major open issue. Its new theorem uses \(O(z_{\mathrm{end}})\) words and \(O(1+\log^2(N/z_{\mathrm{end}}))\) query time, where \(z_{\mathrm{end}}\) counts phrases subject to a different endpoint restriction.
The 2026 grammar trade-off paper explicitly retains efficient access in space linear in ordinary LZ77 size as unknown. Its sharper bounds for grammars do not identify grammar size with LZ77 size.

LZBE supports logarithmic access with linear space in its own factor count, but requires copied material to consist of complete preceding factors. That restriction changes the compressed representation and its size parameter.

sentences: A greedy LZ77 parse stores a string as literals and references to earlier material, including overlapping copies.
The task is to return any chosen character in logarithmic worst-case time while using only a constant number of words per phrase.
All stored input, auxiliary tables and query memory count toward that space bound.
One deterministic construction may use polynomial time in the uncompressed length, and queries cannot consult the uncompressed text.
Results for grammars, LZ-End and LZBE use different compressed-size parameters and do not automatically meet this target.
